items.title: [ScienceDaily] Loneliness is making us sick, but we may be treating it all wrong
items.content_html: Loneliness can be surprisingly deadly, with previous research linking it to a roughly 30% increase in the risk of premature death. However, a new study warns that treating loneliness as a medical condition could distract from its deeper social causes. While healthcare professionals can offer support, lasting solutions may require rebuilding communities and fundamentally changing the way people live and work.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results
items.content_html: Robot-assisted knee replacement surgery offers greater surgical precision, but a landmark clinical trial has revealed a surprising limitation. Despite the advanced technology, patients experienced no meaningful improvements in pain, mobility, or recovery compared with conventional surgery after one year.

items.title: [frontiersin.org] Exercise linked to measurable gains across stroke, heart and lung care
items.content_html: Exercise-based rehabilitation was associated with better quality of life after stroke or transient ischemic attack, greater exercise capacity in heart failure, and measurable changes in small-airway function in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), according to a systematic review, a clinical review and a 62-person study. The evidence differs by condition: the stroke analysis pooled 38 randomized trials, while the COPD study followed participants through a 12-week program combining aerobic and strength exercises. The COPD researchers found clearer changes with impulse oscillometry than with standard spirometry. The heart-failure review said evidence supports fewer short-term hospital admissions from all causes, but effects on heart-failure admissions and mortality remain uncertain. The review also reports that 2026 European Society of Cardiology guidelines recommend cardiac rehabilitation for chronic heart failure with either preserved or reduced ejection fraction.

items.title: 🔓 [NYT Well] What’s Actually in Those Gas Station Drugs?
items.content_html: Inside gas station convenience stores and smoke shops across the country, a new generation of drugs is for sale. It can be difficult to know what’s actually inside these items, which come wrapped in candy-colored packaging and are often readily accessible to the everyday consumer. To better understand this phenomenon, The New York Times purchased and lab-tested 28 products. Matt Richtel, a reporter for Well, walks us through the findings. items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Ozempic is changing the way Americans shop and eat, even if they’ve never taken it
items.content_html:
The new class of drugs led by Ozempic and Wegovy don’t just have transformative effects on the people who take them – they’re reshaping the lives around them too.

Patients prescribed GLP-1s are eating less and drinking less, but those behavioral shifts are trickling down to people in their life who aren’t taking the medications themselves. Nearly one in four U.S. consumers have adjusted the way that they shop, eat, and drink based on knowing other people who take GLP-1s, according to a new survey from market research firm Escalent. 

The survey homed in on a group that the market research group calls “echo consumers,” which refers to people who don’t take a GLP-1 themselves but are changing their habits based on others in their social circles who do. The survey included data from 315 U.S. and 335 U.K. respondents who haven’t taken a GLP-1 drug but know someone who does and report changes to their own behavior based on those social connections.

“Much of the attention surrounding GLP-1 medications has focused on the people taking them, and those living in their households,” Escalent Europe Managing Director Melissa Bane wrote. “… For retailers, food and beverage brands and restaurants, that’s a significant consumer group whose changing habits have gone largely unnoticed.”

Among the echo consumers, 42% reported exercising more, 36% said they consume more wellness products, and 27% are drinking less. When eating out, 49% said they are ordering less at restaurants when eating with someone taking a GLP-1, while 21% are opting for alternative activities instead of socializing while eating and drinking. Almost one in five say they have picked different gifts for GLP-1 users they’ve shopped for, and many say they are buying different food and drinks to bring along to social gatherings in light of smaller appetites and friends and family who aren’t drinking as much.

Industry-shifting numbers

While the new survey only offers a small snapshot of consumer behavior, GLP-1 medications are clearly causing some seismic cultural shifts that we’re only beginning to understand. In the U.S., a massive 11% of the population are currently prescribed GLP-1s and 15% say they have tried them for weight loss before. That huge swath of Americans is already walking, running, and cycling more, buying fewer sweet treats, spending less on groceries, and drinking less alcohol.

Habit shifts among GLP-1 users alone already represent a massive amount of change for industries to adapt to across just a few short years. Beyond those consumers, Escalent’s survey suggests that there are 1.7 times as many people shifting their behavior in light of the widespread use of weight management drugs than there are GLP-1 users. If similar numbers play out in future research, that’s an even more massive chunk of the population suddenly eating, drinking, and buying differently than they did prior to the advent of drugs like Ozempic, Wegovy, and Zepbound.

“For Echo Consumers, a box of chocolates or a bottle of wine may no longer be the gift of choice, and social occasions could increasingly revolve around activities rather than going out for food and drink,” Bane said, calling the changes a “major shift” that will be even more evident during the holiday season. 

“Brands, retailers and hospitality businesses will need to find ways to adapt their offerings to reflect changing demand as these habits continue to spread through social networks.”

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘The only free thing is a bed’: hospital patients forced to pay as Malawi runs out of medicines
items.content_html:
Poor rural families forced to find basic medical supplies as scarcity of foreign exchange paralyses healthcare provision

Two days into her stay at Salima district hospital, Maureen Msukwa is still waiting for a painkiller that the hospital pharmacy cannot provide. In the shade of the acacia trees outside the brick maternity block, dozens of relatives sit on woven mats among plastic buckets, cooking pots and basins of laundry.

Inside, Msukwa, 25, a pregnant mother from Kasache village in central Malawi, clutches a handwritten scrap of paper instructing her to buy paracetamol from a private vendor across the road.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age
items.content_html: A major analysis of 149 studies found that cannabis users develop psychosis an average of 2.5 years earlier than non-users, with the difference growing to more than six years among adults 30 and older. Researchers warn that cannabis-related psychiatric risks may accumulate over time, challenging the belief that using marijuana after adolescence is relatively safe.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
items.content_html: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease
items.content_html: Depression in older adults may be more than a mental health concern. Scientists discovered that accumulating tau protein, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, was linked to worsening depressive symptoms in people who still had normal memory and thinking abilities. The faster tau built up in the brain, the faster depressive symptoms increased, suggesting that mood changes could emerge before cognitive decline.

items.title: [medical.nikkeibp.co.jp] Studies link dementia risk to ADHD and outline prevention measures
items.content_html: A large U.S. cohort study of adults aged 50 and older found that people diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) had higher risks of later mild cognitive impairment or dementia. Published online Oct. 7 in JAMA Psychiatry, the study examined diagnoses in health records alongside genetic risk scores. Separately, updated World Health Organization guidance included, for the first time, offering hearing aids to older adults with hearing loss as part of a strategy to reduce cognitive decline and dementia risk. Spanish neurologist Jorge Máñez said it remains unclear whether physical activity changes the course of Alzheimer’s or Parkinson’s disease, though he cited potential benefits to brain function and vascular health. Russian geriatrician Olga Tkacheva linked flu and pneumococcal vaccination to lower dementia risk, while a Japanese diabetes commentary raised the question of early statin use for prevention.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good
items.content_html: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.

items.title: [bmj.com] UK regulators open mental health AI sandbox to test safety standards
items.content_html: British regulators launched a regulatory sandbox for artificial-intelligence mental-health tools on Nov. 23. Studies have reported screening accuracy and patient use without establishing clinical benefit. The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) and the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) will work with developers, clinicians and people with lived experience to examine evidence and safety challenges; up to five organizations will take part. Hospitals in Kettering and Northampton have used AI software to flag possible abnormalities on chest X-rays since November 2024, while Poland says its public hospital platform now offers five certified imaging models, with clinicians making the final decisions. OpenAI has also made computer-use agents available for health-care administrative workflows, including referrals and prior authorizations. A University of Bath survey found that students are already using generative AI for mental-health support, while a study of 140 pancreatic-cancer patients linked use of a psychological-support feature to lower anxiety and quality-of-life scores; neither establishes that the tools cause better outcomes. The UK sandbox aims to develop practical approaches to evaluating and regulating these technologies.

items.title: [sootoday.com] Canadian study finds daily cannabis use exceeds daily drinking among adults under 50
items.content_html: Daily cannabis use is more common than daily alcohol consumption among Canadian adults under 50, according to a study published Monday in the Canadian Medical Association Journal. Researchers analyzed responses from 99,920 adults in Statistics Canada’s 2023-24 Canadian Community Health Survey: 5.7% reported daily cannabis use, compared with 5.2% for alcohol and 8.5% for cigarettes. The researchers say daily cannabis use is associated with cannabis use disorder, while smoking cannabis poses risks to lung health. About 68% of daily cannabis users reported smoking cannabis, and 41% said they began daily use after legalization. The study relied on self-reported responses and did not distinguish medical from non-medical use.

items.content_html: Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than scientists previously realized, with new research linking lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. The surprising connection suggests that routine medical scans could help uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.
